Mr. President,
excellencies,
distinguished delegates, it is an honor
once again to address this August
assembly on behalf of the government and
people of Tuvalu.
I congratulate his excellency Khalil
Raman of Bangladesh on assuming the role
of the president of the 81st session.
President Raman, you can count on the
full support of Tvalu.
I also congratulate the outgoing
president excellency Analena Bbach of

Mr. President,
to value extends its deepest sympathy
and condolences to all communities
worldwide that are affected by ongoing
armed conflicts and recent natural
disasters, including the devastating
floods in Nepal and Myanmar, the
earthquake in Colombia, and the tragic
loss of lives at sea in Banuatu.
Touvalu reiterates its hope for peace,
stability, and the unimpeded
humanitarian relief and reaffirms its
solidarity with all those facing
violence, insecurity, and lost.
Mr. President, in less than a week,
Touvalu will celebrate its 48th
anniversary of independence,
a significant milestone as Tovalu
approaches its golden jubilee of
independence.
On this month, Tvalu also celebrates its
26th
anniversary of UN membership.
to value reaffirms its strong commitment
to the values and the principle of the
UN charter and to international law and
to a multilateral system that protects
the dignity and security of all people.
This year also marks the historical and
first deployment of Tvalu police
officers to serve in the UN mission in
South Sudan.
A deployment that confirms that even the
smallest member of the UN can contribute
meaningfully to international peace and
security.
Mr. President,
the theme for this session, restoring
trust, managing transformation, a United
Nations that delivers for all, resonates
well with the moment of time we find
ourselves in right now. There is no
denying that the architecture of
multilateralism
and international law founded on the UN
charter is under enormous stress and
restoring that trust in that
architecture is critical particularly
for small island developing states like
Touvalu whose sovereignty and future are
anchored in that very architecture.
Touvalu therefore stands in solidarity
with fellow member states in contri
contributing to the restoration of that
trust and advancing the necessary
reforms and transformation that will
enable the United Nation to deliver for
all. Mr. President Touvalu like other
countries is being challenged by various
enforced transformations that threaten
our land, values, knowledge, and
cultures.
Climate change is transforming our
physical environment.
Technology is transforming how we
communicate, govern, and preserve
knowledge. artificial intelligence is
changing the way economies and society
uh function.
The challenge is not to stop
transformation.
Rather, the challenge is to manage
transformation in a manner that protect
people, preserve what is valuable and
give every country the capacity to
determine its own future.
In response to the transformation to
Touvalu's physical environment caused by
rising seas, the Touvalu coastal
adaptation project TCAP has already
reclaimed on the capital island of
Funafuti 15.3
of elevated and flat-free land as part
of the reinforcement of the island's
coastal uh areas.
A further 10 he actors is being
reclaimed which is significant
adjustment for a country with only 26
square kilometers of land area.
While we work to protect our physical
territory, we are also contemplating
preserving the intangible foundations of
our nation, our traditional values,
knowledge and cultures.
In that regard, we have two digital
initiatives. The first is the tovalu
digital nation initiative that utilizes
digital technologies to sustain our
sovereignty institutions and our
capacity to deliver services to enhance
to ensure that our national identity is
not lost in the transformation. The
second is the Tovalu digital arc
initiative which seeks to preserve
Tovalu's culture and historical heritage
in digital form.
Mr. President,
less than 24 hours ago, member states
endorsed in this very building the
landmark United Nation political
declaration on sea level rise. A
monumental and gratifying achievement
for Tuvalu because Tuvalu was at the
forefront of global efforts demanding
such a declaration. For Tuvalu, sea
level rise is not a future threat. It is
a present reality. Tovalu is therefore
overwhelmed with joy and warmly welcome
the commitments the declaration
entails. Namely, firstly, it affirms the
continuity of statehood and sovereignty
despite sea level rise. Secondly, it
safeguards the permanence of maritime
zones and rights established under the
UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Thirdly, it recognize and protects the
rights, dignity, culture, identity and
heritage of affected people.
Fourthly, it commits to strengthened
adaptation and resilience.
Fifthly, it calls for accessible,
predictable and needsbased climate
finance. And sixthly, and it supports
science, technology, data, and knowledge
systems that enable informed decision
making and long-term planning for
vulnerable countries. The declaration
affirms that Tvalu's nationhood is not
negotiable, that our maritime rights are
not erasable, and that our people should
never be forced to choose between their
homeland and their future. Mr. President
for the sustainable development goals SG

because the consequences of such

President,
climate change is and remains the the
single greatest existential threat to
Tovalu's survival, security, and
sustainable development.
Touvalu acknowledges the efforts of the
international community to address the
climate crisis, but the pace and scale
of global actions remain insufficient.
With a temporary overshoot of the 1.5
degree Celsius target now inevitable,
a fast, fair, just, and orderly
transition away from fossil fuel is even
more urgent and require serious
attention. Although the science may be
clear that methane mitigation is the
only scalable near-term solution capable
of rapidly slowing global temperature
rise and buying time for long-term CO2
decarbonization strategies to take
effect. Tuvalu will insist that CO2
mitigation must also remain a top
priority and that both methane
mitigation and CO2 mitigation should be
v vigorously pursued simultaneously.
Therefore, the Daserigi call for a
fossil fuel-f free Pacific and the
Fafuti call for climate justice and
climate actions, a critical Pacific
instrument championing Pacific regional
survival and global climate actions.
Towards that objective, Tvalu is
determined to play its part in driving
greater ambition, including the hosting
of the leader segment event of the
pre-COP uh 31 next month and co-hosting
uh with Ireland and Tovalu next year,
the second conference on transitioning
away from fossil fuel. Touvalu reminds
states of their legal obligation to take
appropriate action to protect the
climate system from greenhouse gas
emissions as failure to do so constitute
an internationally wrongful act as
confirmed by the ICJ advisory opinion.
Touvalu welcomes the operationalization
of the loss and damage fund and call on
countries to honor their pledges and
commitments.
Adequate, predictable and timely
financing is essential to ensure the
fund can fully deliver on its mandate
and provide meaningful support to those
most vulnerable to climate related loss
and damage, including non-economic loss
and damage.
Finance therefore must be provided as
grants at the scale required to address
the climate impacts already unavoidable
and the increasing lost and damage
caused by further warming. Tvalu stands
ready to work with all nations to
advance climate ambitions uh strengthen
resilience and ensure that no country is
left behind. Tovalu's message is clear.
The world must act now and decisively,
collectively, and with urgency to
protect the future for generations to
come. Mr. President,
the ocean is central to Tovalu's
identity and sustainable uh development.
The ocean has sustained Tuvalu for
generations and remains at the heart of
our existence, our future and our
resilience. Touvalu may have only 26
square kilometers of land, but we are
custodians of some 750,000
square kilometers of ocean, which makes
Touvalu a large ocean state. This year,
Touvalu soft launched its first ever
national ocean policy, a comprehensive
framework to strengthen our stewardship
of marine resources, affirm the
permanence of our maritime zones,
protect biodiversity,
and place the ocean at the center of our
resilience and sustainable development.
We thank all of our partners whose
invaluable support helped turn this
national vision into reality. For
Tuvalu, ocean governance is not simply
an environmental policy. It is also an
issue of economic security, food
security and climate uh security. Tovalu
has ratified the BB&J agreement and look
forwards to contributing to the first
conference of the parties of the
agreement next year. to values objective
towards the implementation of the BB&J
is simple in that the ocean areas beyond
national jurisdictions belong to our
shared future and must be governed
responsibly based on science equity the
precautionary approach and effective
international cooperation
Mr. President Tovalu like other small
island developing states is highly
vulnerable to climate and economic
shocks but the international financing
architecture is illequipped to respond
effectively to those shocks. Earlier
this year, Touvalu declared a national
state of emergency due to prolonged
electrical power disruptions caused by
fuel shortages, escalating energy cost,
and infrastructural deficiency.
Although Touvalu did uh receive with
gratitude external assistance, the
timing and scale of those responses were
slow and inefficient. And this is why
access to rapid dispersement and crisis
response financing is essential for the
stability and resilience of small island
developing state. Tvalu therefore
continues to urge the international
community to adopt financial approaches
that match the urgency of the crisis
with similar simpler and faster access
to climate finance. scaled up adaptation
funding, accessible loss and damaged uh
finance and rapid dispersement crisis
mechanism.
Mr. President, in the Pacific, Pacific
leaders have adopted the Pacific
Resilience Facility, a regional
financing mechanism to help our
communities respond effectively to the
growing impact of climate change.
Touvalu calls on the international
community and our development partners
to support the full capitalization of
the Pacific Resilience Facility to
enable Pacific lead and Pacific own
solutions to build resilience where it
matters most.
Mr. President, adaptation and building
resilience against the impact of climate
change will reduce the severity of
climate change, but will not eliminate
all consequences of climate change. One
of those consequences is people deciding
to migrate and set up home elsewhere.
Although relocation is not part of
Tvalu's climate change strategy, it is
inevitable that some Tvaluan may decide
to migrate and it is incumbent on the
government to ensure that they do so
with dignity. Toval therefore endorse
the global principle for climate mo for
climate uh mobility which are
rightsbased, people centered and
grounded in international law. We invite
all member states and partner to join us
in advancing this framework of
cooperation and common ambition.
Mr. President,
as we call for a multilateral system
that delivers for all nations, we must
also uphold the principles of dignity,
inclusion, and equality for all the
people.
Yet too many communities remain outside
the structures designed to serve all
humanity. Tovalu therefore calls for
arrangements that enable the meaningful
participation of the 23.3 million people
of Taiwan in the United Nation and its
specialized agencies and mechanism.
Taiwan has consistently demonstrated
that it is an able, trustworthy, and a
constructive partner in addressing
global challenges, and its exclusion
undermines both the spirit and
effectiveness of multilateral
cooperation.
Touvalu is also gravely concerned by the
escalating military activities around
Taiwan, which threatens stability across
the Taiwan Strait, disrupt international
transportation and trade, and jeopardize
peace and security in the Pacific and
beyond. We commend Taiwan for its calm
and principled adherence to the values
of the UN charter. and we urge all
member state to uphold the same
principles. At the same time, uh,
Touvalu remains troubled by the
long-standing unilateral economic
measures imposed on Cupa. These
restrictions continue to inflict
hardship on the Cupend people,
contravene the human rights commitment
of the UN and run counter to the
cooperative spirit of the 2030 agenda
for sustainable development. The
continuation of those economic sanctions
deprive Cuper of essential development
partnership and support needed for
recovery and future progress. and we
call for the lifting of those sanctions.
Touvalu also support the call for
necessary reform uh of the UN security
council to ensure that it is more
representative, inclusive, transparent
and accountable and better align it with
the reality of the 21st geopolitical
uh landscape. Mr. President to conclude
I wish to assure this assembly that
Touvalu stands in solidarity with the
rest of the member state to play its
part in restoring trust and managing
transformation to ensure the United
Nation delivers for all. Tvalu has shown
that small nations can lead in climate
adaptation and resilience, ocean
stewardship, digital innovation,
mobility with dignity, and the
advancement of international law.
Tovalu's ability to lead is not
determined by the extent of our
vulnerability. But national leadership
cannot substitute for global
responsibility.
The United Nation and its charter are
the bedrock of international cooperation
and multilateralism
and they must be guarded with all
seriousness and integrity. Tvalu will
continue to stand firm in its effort to
safeguard its sovereignty, the health of
the ocean and the integrity of its
people despite climate change and under
global transformation because they are
worth fighting for. and Touvalu invites
this assembly to stand with us in that
fight. Touvalu thanks the outgoing
secretary general for his exceptional
and exemplary leadership and wish him
well in his retirement and other future
endeavors. I thank you and fafasi tovalu
